title: The rod (Sn 4.15)
hookLine: read it again, whole: fear born from the rod
tomorrow: alone in an empty place, what is there to be afraid of?

lines: FEAR IS BORN FROM THE ROD.
cards: Keys pushed out between the knuckles on a dark walk home. A phone squeezed during a call that's going badly. A jaw set hard before a meeting.

The hand knows fear before the mind names it. The fifteenth poem of the chapter of eights gives its guess about where fear begins, and it may not be the first place you'd look. Fear, it says, is born from the rod.
Not only from the rod raised against you. From the one you pick up.

teach.h: DANDA: A STICK, A WEAPON, A BLOW.
teach.b: The rod here is danda: a stick, a weapon, a blow. The poem, Sutta Nipata 4.15, opens: fear is born from taking up the rod; look at people fighting. And then the Buddha turns to his own story.
I will tell you, he says, how dread came over me.

I saw people floundering like fish in a little water, turning on one another, and fear came. The world had no core; every direction was shaken. I looked for a place to live that no one had already claimed, and found none.
Hear the sound of that: fish thrashing in a shrinking pool, all of them crowded, all of them at odds.

Then, he says, I saw a dart, hard to see, lodged in the heart. Whoever is pierced by it runs in every direction; pull it out, and you don't run and you don't sink. So the rod and the fear are one loop.
The grip makes the fear, and the fear makes the grip.

A detail worth passing on: the same Pali word stands in a verse of the Dhammapada, where Max Müller translates it punishment: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter."

how: Theravada teachers often read this poem as the Buddha's own account of the urgency that sent him seeking, and pair it with the first of the five precepts, to refrain from harming living beings.

o: a teacher's staff, passed down to a student
the measuring stick for a monk's robe and bowl
the weapon taken up, and the fear it breeds

p: a stick, a weapon, a blow
hard to see; makes you run

s: the poem says fear only comes from the rod someone raises against you
it starts with taking up the rod: the grip makes the fear, and the fear makes the grip.
in this poem the Buddha tells how fear came over him
he saw people floundering like fish in a little water, turning on one another.

games.q: a neighbor's dog barks at night, and you've drafted a sharp note for their door that ends with a threat to call the city. what does the rod poem point toward?
o: set the threat down first, then write what you need without it.
send it as is; a firm threat is the only thing that ends a fight.
say nothing at all, ever; putting down the rod means no requests.
games.why: the poem says fear is born from taking up the rod. you can still ask; putting down the rod means asking without the weapon in your hand.

practice: Pick up something small near you, a pen, a spoon, a key, and grip it hard for three breaths. Feel it in the fingers, the wrist, the forearm, maybe the jaw.
Then set it down slowly, open the hand on your knee, and spend the rest of the sit feeling the difference travel up the arm.

wordCard.voice: The rod: the stick or weapon taken up, Pali danda, in Sutta Nipata 4.15. The poem traces fear back to the grip, and the grip back to a dart in the heart.

orig.note: Pali: rod, stick, weapon, punishment. Fear is born from taking it up.

carryVoice: Something to keep in your hand, or out of it: put down the rod. Day sixteen-seventy, set down.
